key_finding: A nudge that shrouds the autopay-minimum option cut minimum-only payments by 23% after six months but did not reduce credit card debt, and it raised missed payments by reducing autopay enrollment overall.
methodology: Field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment, six-month follow-up, large administrative panel of cardholders.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the internal premise that steering enrollment automatically improves real financial outcomes: it shows a default-style nudge shifted nominal behavior without improving the underlying goal, and even created harm (missed payments) via liquidity-constrained users — exactly the disengagement/complaint risk the support team is worried about for round-up.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
shrouding a repayment option, not an enrolment/entry decision per se
relevance_reason: A rare consumer, self-directed, liquid-money field experiment showing a default-like nudge can raise nominal compliance while failing the substantive goal and harming a liquidity-constrained subgroup.

key_finding: A state-of-the-art synthesis of DC plan design shows automatic enrollment and default investment options have well-documented short- and longer-term effects, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative overview of the defined-contribution plan design literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a synthesis-level view of the engagement cost of automatic enrollment that mirrors the support team's objection, but it is scoped to employer 401(k) design rather than a consumer app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
narrative overview without a systematic protocol or new effect sizes
relevance_reason: Broad synthesis of default/auto-enrollment effects and engagement costs, useful as background but off the brief's consumer setting.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term retirement plan participation but induces behavioral inertia — low default contribution rates, inactive account management, and churn — undermining long-term welfare gains.
methodology: Narrative discussion/commentary piece, no new data. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Restates the passivity/disengagement concern in general terms but adds no new effect sizes or consumer-app evidence beyond what other shortlisted papers already establish more rigorously.
limitations: employer retirement system framing, not consumer product
no empirical effect sizes, zero citations, general commentary rather than original research
relevance_reason: Echoes the brief's counter-argument about passive enrollment and disengagement but with weak evidentiary weight.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for how default effects persist or fade downstream, identifying time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as the key moderators of whether a default's effect lasts.
methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework paper covering the consumer-defaults literature; research agenda, not primary data. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to predict when the round-up default's enrollment lift will or won't persist at 6-12 months, and what to measure (antecedent savings intent, trade-off salience) to distinguish nominal from real engagement.
limitations: theoretical/taxonomic, not an empirical effect size
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Directly targets the persistence-of-defaults question central to the brief, in a general consumer (not employer) frame, and proposes measurable moderators.

key_finding: Using natural experiments and random assignment to default options in Medicare Part D, beneficiary passivity was extremely insensitive even when the default caused substantial losses, with active-choice variation driven by transitory shocks rather than attentiveness.
methodology: Natural experiments plus random assignment to default options in a large administrative Medicare Part D dataset.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that people stick with harmful defaults even under high stakes, useful caution for how sticky a poorly-chosen preset multiplier could become, but the population (low-income Medicare beneficiaries choosing drug plans) is a different decision structure from a banking app.
limitations: healthcare/insurance enrollment, not consumer financial savings
low-income Medicare population differs from general banking app users
relevance_reason: Rigorous evidence on default insensitivity and passivity mechanisms, relevant by analogy to whether users would passively stick with a harmful preset, but in an off-domain policy setting.

key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, medium- and long-run dynamics (job separation, withdrawal on separation, auto-escalation opt-out) shrink the effect of automatic enrollment and auto-escalation to just 0.6% and 0.3% of income respectively, with only 40% escalating on the first date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of automatic savings policies across nine 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative statement of the support team's objection: initial enrollment lift from defaults is real but substantially eroded over time by opt-outs and withdrawals, directly bearing on whether the round-up enrollment number will be vanity.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated setting, not a self-directed banking app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving in the medium/long run, the single most load-bearing finding for the brief's persistence question.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into the public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most people actively opted back out, with stronger default effects when incentives were higher or knowledge of enrollment status was lower.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around a nationwide auto-enrollment policy change.
why_it_matters: Quantifies a large default effect size and shows it is contingent on incentive strength and awareness — useful benchmark for expected enrollment lift, but the mechanism (compulsory public pension, government trust) does not map to a discretionary banking app feature.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, government intermediary not a bank app
no data on persistence of savings amounts, only enrollment status
relevance_reason: Gives a clean default effect size and shows sensitivity to incentives/awareness, directly analogous to the entry decision but in an employer/government-mediated pension context.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months across 100+ US plans and a UK panel, is substantially attenuated by 36 months, though it still reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the gap between short-run enrollment lift and medium-run savings amount gains that the brief asks about, though the switching-cost framework and 401(k) setting are pension-specific rather than a liquid banking app.
limitations: employer/national retirement plans, not a discretionary consumer app
structural model estimates depend on switching-cost assumptions not directly observed
relevance_reason: Best available empirical answer to whether default gains persist and whether they change amounts saved versus who is nominally enrolled, even though the setting is retirement plans.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person study across five European countries, default risk-allocation nudges produced medium-to-large effects on risk-taking but also lowered ratings of the advisor's honesty and advice quality, especially when the default was refused, and framing of the default question itself shifted allocation choices.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments including a large representative multi-country European sample, manipulating default presence and framing in an investment-allocation context.
why_it_matters: Provides EU-specific evidence that a preset allocation/multiplier can anchor choices strongly (informing the level decision) while also damaging perceived trustworthiness when the default is refused — a direct test of when a default reads as manipulative in exactly this regulatory context.
limitations: wealth-management advice context rather than a round-up savings feature specifically
risk allocation rather than savings-rate multiplier as the anchored quantity
relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-advice setting giving effect sizes for anchoring on preset levels and quantifying the reputational/trust cost of defaults, squarely answering both the level-anchoring and manipulation-risk questions.

key_finding: With automatic 401(k) enrollment, participation exceeded 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still anchored to both after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large US firms following automatic enrollment adoption.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a preset level anchors most people's chosen contribution rate for years, which is the foundational evidence the anchoring literature and the round-up multiplier decision both build on and argue with.
limitations: employer 401(k) context, not a consumer app
no year given in metadata; predates the app/liquidity/regulatory context the brief flags as changed
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring-on-defaults study that current work (including several other shortlisted papers) directly responds to.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost, and adding an intermediate option to an existing default menu captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at modest revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping transactions, combined with an independent stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Offers a transferable mechanism — friction complementarity between deviation cost and opt-out cost — and a concrete design lesson (adding an intermediate preset can capture most of the welfare gain) directly applicable to designing the 1x/2x/5x round-up menu.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings enrollment
single transactional choice, no persistence or engagement measured
relevance_reason: Provides a structural mechanism for why preset menus anchor choices and a concrete example of adding an intermediate default option, directly informing the multiplier-menu design question.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term (liquid, withdrawable anytime) payroll-deduction savings program at five UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a balance and 87% received a contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of account activation and usage data from a UK employer short-term savings program over its first 12 months.
why_it_matters: The closest existing analogue to the round-up feature (short-term, liquid, opt-in savings) shows opt-in yields very low take-up but strong retention among adopters — direct evidence against the vanity-metric fear for those who do opt in, though it says nothing about opt-out enrollment.
limitations: employer payroll intermediary, which the brief says does not carry over to a self-directed app
no opt-out or active-choice arm to compare against
relevance_reason: Near-identical product structure (liquid opt-in short-term savings) to the round-up feature, giving real retention numbers for opt-in adopters, despite the employer-channel mismatch.

key_finding: A general theoretical characterization shows that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions for externalities, Pigouvian fees, and disagreement about value.
methodology: Theoretical/computational modeling of optimal default design with numerical simulations verifying asymptotic approximations. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers normative design principles for when opting people out of an unwanted default (vs. minimizing it) is welfare-optimal, relevant to deciding whether opt-out enrollment is justified when the bank and users may disagree about round-up's value.
limitations: purely theoretical with simulated rather than empirical validation
no named population or product setting to ground applicability
relevance_reason: General normative framework for optimal default design that bears on whether opt-out is justified given possible designer/user disagreement about round-up savings' value.

key_finding: EU dark-pattern law protects consumer autonomy, and the paper develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations applicable to choice-architecture practices like pre-selected defaults.
methodology: Legal doctrinal analysis mapping EU dark-pattern statutes and case law; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete legal framework for testing whether an opt-out round-up default would read as an autonomy-violating dark pattern under EU law, directly bearing on the reputational/legal risk flagged in the brief.
limitations: no empirical effect sizes
normative/legal analysis rather than behavioral evidence
abstract-only
relevance_reason: Directly addresses when a default is helpful versus manipulative under EU law, the exact reputational-risk question the brief raises for the opt-out design.

key_finding: A 12% default contribution rate led 25% of employees to remain unopted-out at 12 months (versus ~50% at lower defaults), and many stayed at the suboptimal 12% rate rather than the employer-match-optimizing level.
methodology: Field data analysis of an employer's 401(k) plan with an unusually high default rate, benchmarked against a literature review of lower-default plans.
why_it_matters: Provides direct evidence that a preset contribution level anchors participants even when suboptimal, the core mechanism behind our multiplier pre-selection decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer liquid savings app
no randomization
employer-as-trusted-intermediary mechanism does not transfer to our setting
relevance_reason: Clearest available evidence on anchoring at a preset default level, directly informing the multiplier pre-selection decision.

key_finding: Abstract text is unavailable; the title indicates field experiments testing automated short-term payroll savings across four large U.K. programs.
methodology: abstract-only (abstract text is corrupted/missing); title suggests large-scale field experiments.
why_it_matters: Could speak to short-term, liquid savings automation effects analogous to round-up savings, but no usable evidence is available to act on.
limitations: abstract text missing/corrupted, preventing assessment of effect sizes or population fit
relevance_reason: Title suggests direct relevance to short-term liquid savings automation, but content could not be verified.

key_finding: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft SMS alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks testing automatic enrollment into text alert features.
why_it_matters: Same institutional setting and mechanism (auto-enrolling users into a helpful account feature inside a consumer bank's app) as our round-up decision, giving a realistic benchmark effect size for automatic enrollment.
limitations: studies overdraft alerts, not a savings feature, so behavior and amounts differ
no measurement of long-term disengagement or opt-out from the alert feature
relevance_reason: Same consumer-banking auto-enrollment mechanism and institutional context as our product, with concrete effect sizes on a comparable feature.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment raised savings but each additional month also increased unsecured debt by about £7 alongside £32-38 in pension savings, partially offsetting the net benefit.
methodology: Randomized nationwide roll-out of UK pension automatic enrollment to ~160,000 small employers, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Shows a default-driven rise in nominal savings can be partly offset by other financial behavior, undercutting the assumption that higher enrollment automatically means unambiguous consumer benefit.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension context rather than self-directed consumer app
savings are illiquid/locked, unlike a round-up pot
relevance_reason: Contradicts the simple premise that defaults raise net financial benefit, relevant to whether enrollment numbers would be a vanity metric.

key_finding: Removing auto-enrollment and adding an enrollment 'ordeal' reduced health-insurance enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment policy in a health-insurance selection market, with a supporting selection model.
why_it_matters: Rigorous evidence that enrollment friction (the opposite of a default) falls unevenly on disadvantaged groups, directly relevant to the brief's question of who is helped or hurt by enrollment design.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a consumer savings product
adverse-selection dynamics specific to insurance may not map onto a savings feature
relevance_reason: Rigorous distributional evidence on how enrollment friction disproportionately harms disadvantaged users.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest effect on small, inexperienced donors who likely did not intend to give recurringly.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across political campaign websites exploiting the timing of default rollout.
why_it_matters: Shows opt-out defaults on financial commitments can generate large nominal uptake while causing real harm concentrated among the least sophisticated users, exactly the vanity-enrollment/complaint risk the support team raises.
limitations: political donations, not a banking savings product
short observation window relative to the brief's 6-12 month persistence question
relevance_reason: Near-identical mechanism (opt-out default on a recurring financial contribution) with direct evidence of harm to naive users.

key_finding: In a lab search experiment, a default option raises the reservation utility via a reference effect leading to better choices, while those who reject the default and search actively tend to find higher-ranked alternatives.
methodology: Theoretical model plus lab experiments on reference-dependent search behavior with a default option.
why_it_matters: Offers a general behavioral mechanism for why active choosers might outperform passive default-takers, background for evaluating active choice versus default framing.
limitations: generic lab search task unrelated to financial products or savings apps
abstract-only
relevance_reason: General mechanism for default versus active-choice quality differences, but in an unrelated experimental-economics setting.

key_finding: EU Digital Markets Act browser choice screens raised Firefox usage 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting at least 15 months post-rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered rollout of DMA-mandated choice screens across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Real-world evidence, in the exact EU regulatory and mobile-app context of the brief, that forced active choice produces large and durable shifts away from a default, directly informing how much benefit an active-choice onboarding screen could capture.
limitations: studies browser selection, not financial or savings behavior
choice-screen implementation details may not transfer to an app-onboarding active-choice screen
relevance_reason: Same EU regulatory mobile-app context, directly measuring active-choice-screen effects with long persistence, the clearest evidence for the active-choice comparison decision.

key_finding: A usability study of nine active-choice (no-default) privacy opt-out interface designs found that generalizable schemes reduced disruption (98% not feeling disrupted for the best scheme, a 40-point improvement) with only a slight loss in opt-out utility.
methodology: Browser-extension usability study with 410 participants comparing nine active-choice, default-free opt-out interface designs.
why_it_matters: Offers a concrete UI approach to making an active-choice, no-default flow feel low-friction, relevant to designing a forced active-choice onboarding screen without frustrating users.
limitations: privacy opt-out setting, not a financial/savings product
legally mandated no-default requirement differs from our discretionary design choice
relevance_reason: Concrete active-choice interface design evidence relevant to a forced-choice onboarding screen, though from a different regulatory domain.

key_finding: An opt-out default for exam sign-up increased sign-ups, but increased actual exam completion/passing only for students who were previously responsive to university communication; non-responsive students showed higher nominal sign-up with no effect on the effortful outcome.
methodology: Two field experiments switching university exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out, tracking sign-up, participation, and pass rates.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences that a default can inflate nominal enrollment without changing the effortful behavior it's meant to produce, and that this varies by user responsiveness, echoing the support team's vanity-metric concern.
limitations: university exam context, not a financial product
effort here is academic rather than monetary engagement
relevance_reason: Empirically shows defaults can raise nominal sign-up while leaving effortful target behavior unchanged for some users.

key_finding: After a policy change let target-date funds become default retirement investments, younger workers' stock allocations shifted to follow the TDF glidepath, while contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel analysis of millions of U.S. retirement investors, 2006-2018, around a default-investment policy change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can reshape one downstream choice (allocation) while leaving an untargeted parameter (contribution rate) largely unchanged, a caution for whether presetting the multiplier alone would spill over to other saving behavior.
limitations: employer retirement investment defaults, not a consumer round-up multiplier
asset-allocation choice differs structurally from a contribution-level choice
relevance_reason: Marginally informs anchoring/spillover reasoning but in a distant employer-investment setting.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary Chinese pension saving, all tested nudges, including default options, significantly reduced willingness to contribute and share of income saved, with default and positive-narrative nudges backfiring most, varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that defaults reliably lift enrollment or contribution, showing defaults can backfire, with effects that vary by demographic group.
limitations: small online-survey sample (n=220) measuring stated willingness rather than real behavior
Chinese cultural/institutional context differs from the EU app setting
voluntary pension rather than liquid consumer savings
relevance_reason: The clearest available contradiction of 'defaults always help', directly answering the brief's request for a paper pushing against that premise.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people rated financial nudges positively overall, preferred reflective (System 2) interventions and savings-framed messages, and transparency did not reduce approval.
methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment with 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting; representative Australian sample, n=2,100.
why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial nudge or default is perceived as manipulative versus helpful — savings framing and reflective design raise approval — informing how we message the round-up default so it doesn't read as a dark pattern.
limitations: Hypothetical scenarios rather than actual enrolment behaviour
Australian sample, not EU regulatory context
No measure of enrolment rate or amount saved
relevance_reason: Speaks directly to the manipulation/dark-pattern risk question the brief flags for EU consumer protection.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries the choice to receive transfers via bank account had no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances among those with no prior savings.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among conditional cash transfer beneficiaries in Chile comparing cash versus bank-account delivery of subsidies.
why_it_matters: Shows a choice about where money is held does not reliably raise savings on average, only for the subgroup with the least prior savings — a caution against assuming choice architecture alone changes amount saved.
limitations: Developing-country CCT population, not a consumer banking app user base
About account choice for transfers, not round-up enrolment defaults
No multi-year persistence data
relevance_reason: Near-setting evidence on whether a savings-account choice changes actual amounts saved rather than just nominal enrolment.

key_finding: Abstract-only fragment comparing contribution levels and fund liquidity under an automatic IRA plan design with an emergency-savings feature.
methodology: abstract-only
why_it_matters: Touches on liquid emergency-savings features attached to automatic enrolment, adjacent to the round-up pot's own liquidity, but gives no usable effect sizes.
limitations: Abstract too sparse to extract findings
Employer/government-sponsored IRA context, not a consumer banking app
No stated effect sizes or persistence data
relevance_reason: Adjacent topic (automatic enrolment plus liquid savings) but abstract gives nothing to act on.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan to automatic enrolment dramatically raised participation, and most automatically-enrolled employees stuck to the default contribution rate and fund allocation even years later.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment using administrative 401(k) records at a large U.S. corporation.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that default enrolment lifts participation and that a pre-set level anchors most participants — sets the baseline against which the round-up default decision should be measured.
limitations: Employer-mediated retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
Locked, illiquid savings unlike a round-up pot
2001 data predates today's fintech and regulatory context
relevance_reason: The classic default-and-anchoring result the current literature (and this brief) argues with.

key_finding: Abstract unavailable; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviours between automatically-enrolled and voluntarily-enrolled defined-contribution retirement plan participants.
methodology: abstract-only
why_it_matters: Could bear on whether auto-enrolment changes savings amount versus just enrolment, but no findings are stated to evaluate.
limitations: No abstract provided, cannot assess methodology or results
Employer-sponsored DC plan, not a consumer round-up product
Forthcoming publication, not yet peer-verified
relevance_reason: Title matches the enrolment-vs-behaviour question but the abstract gives nothing to act on.

key_finding: Limited trust in financial institutions and minority/non-national status predicted both under-saving and early withdrawal from a mandatory pension scheme, based on three national surveys around an Estonian pension-freedom reform.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020–2022) around a policy reform introducing early-withdrawal rights.
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the support team's concern — passively accumulated savings get withdrawn early — and identifies which users are most likely to disengage or withdraw, informing who the round-up feature could end up harming.
limitations: Mandatory pension scheme, not a liquid consumer savings product
Cross-sectional/survey design, not a controlled default-enrolment experiment
Estonian-specific institutional trust context
relevance_reason: Directly relevant to the persistence/withdrawal and distributional-harm questions the brief raises, even though the setting is pensions not fintech.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrolment vaccination policy reduced their stated compliance intentions and their approval of the policy.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries testing reflection prompts on a hypothetical opt-out enrolment policy.
why_it_matters: Shows surfacing a default to people can backfire — reducing both compliance and approval — a warning that a visible opt-out enrolment for round-up savings could trigger disapproval rather than passive acceptance.
limitations: Vaccination policy domain, not a financial or consumer setting
Hypothetical scenario, not actual product enrolment
No amount-saved or persistence outcome measured
relevance_reason: Contradicts the assumption that defaults are simply accepted; a relevant warning for backlash risk in an EU consumer context, though the domain is non-financial.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment and employer matching were associated with higher retirement-plan participation among Millennials in the 2018 FINRA survey, while their absence predicted non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis (FINRA Millennial Investment Study, 2018) with regression controls for debt, income, and risk tolerance.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the standard default-enrolment participation lift in a modern cohort, but adds little beyond what is already established for employer-mediated plans.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a self-directed consumer app
Correlational survey design, no causal identification
No data on amount saved, persistence, or active-choice comparison
relevance_reason: Confirms the standard default effect but in the wrong setting and without new mechanism or effect-size precision for this decision.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish savings records, each $1 of subsidy raised total saving by only 1 cent (mostly reshuffled by the 15% of 'active' savers), while automatic employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation among the 85% of 'passive' savers.
methodology: Administrative panel data covering the population of Denmark, exploiting variation in subsidy and automatic-contribution policies.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that passive (default) mechanisms move real savings amounts while opt-in incentives mostly reshuffle existing assets — directly bears on whether an opt-out round-up default raises net savings and flags that the financially sophisticated respond to choice while everyone else needs the default.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged account system via employer and government policy, not a liquid consumer round-up feature
Contribution decisions are far less liquid/reversible than a round-up pot
No forced active-choice condition tested, only active vs passive response to subsidy
relevance_reason: Best-available large-scale effect-size and distributional evidence on active vs passive savings mechanisms, directly informing the entry-design trade-off despite a pensions setting.

key_finding: Across several studies and two field experiments, an 'enhanced active choice' design — where the required choice highlights losses from the non-preferred option — outperformed plain active choice and is proposed as an alternative to automatic enrolment where opt-out defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Literature review plus a series of studies, including two field experiments, comparing active choice, enhanced active choice, and default/opt-out designs.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, testable design for the entry decision: a forced-choice screen framed around the loss of not rounding up, capturing most of the opt-out enrolment lift without defaulting people in — exactly the trade-off the brief asks about.
limitations: Field experiments are in health/medication-adherence settings, not financial products
No direct comparison to opt-out enrolment on a savings product
No data on persistence or amount saved over 6–12 months
relevance_reason: The enhanced-active-choice technique is a directly transferable design pattern for the entry decision, not merely an analogous finding.

key_finding: This overview chapter synthesizes behavioral household-finance evidence on consumption and savings and reviews choice-architecture interventions — defaults, product design, disclosure — that firms and governments use to shape financial behaviour.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter (NBER).
why_it_matters: Provides the cross-study synthesis the brief asks for, grounding both the entry and level decisions in the broader behavioural household-finance evidence base rather than a single study's estimate.
limitations: Broad overview rather than a study of round-up savings specifically
Synthesizes mostly employer-plan and general household-finance literature
Abstract gives no specific quantitative effect sizes for a fintech round-up context
relevance_reason: The synthesis/review the brief explicitly asked for, situating effect sizes and mechanisms in context rather than one study's estimate.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of new participants stuck with the low default contribution rate (2–3%) and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years, largely offsetting the participation gain's effect on wealth accumulation.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing automatic versus opt-in 401(k) enrolment.
why_it_matters: The clearest evidence that a pre-set default level anchors most users for years — warning that whichever round-up multiplier we pre-select will likely become the de facto level for most enrolled users, potentially offsetting the enrolment gain in actual amount saved.
limitations: Employer-mediated illiquid retirement account, not a liquid consumer round-up pot
Early-2000s data before current app/regulatory context
No active-choice comparison arm
relevance_reason: Directly answers whether a preset level anchors contribution choice — core to the multiplier decision — despite the account type differing from ours.

key_finding: Randomly assigning Afghan employees to default enrolment in a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of choosing, and it also increased later voluntary saving.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with multiple treatment arms isolating mechanisms behind the default effect, salary-linked savings accounts, Afghanistan.
why_it_matters: Identifies why defaults work (present bias, cognitive cost of choosing) rather than just that they work, and shows the effect can persist into later active choices — evidence for judging whether active choice alone could substitute for a default by targeting the same frictions.
limitations: Salary-linked accounts for employees in a developing-country context, not a EU consumer banking app
No 6–12 month withdrawal or disengagement outcome reported
Different liquidity and regulatory environment
relevance_reason: Best mechanism-level evidence for why default effects occur, useful for judging whether active choice can substitute for a default.

key_finding: A reminder nudge for credit card payments reduced late-payment fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%; users with a history of overdraft use saw a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, tracking downstream fee outcomes across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' question: a well-intentioned choice-architecture intervention can net-harm the exact subgroup (already financially stretched, prone to overdraft/withdrawal) most analogous to the passively-enrolled, disengaged users the support team worries about — this should shape what heterogeneity we monitor post-launch, not just aggregate enrolment.
limitations: Brazilian consumer credit/checking market, not EU round-up savings
studies a reminder nudge, not an enrolment default or preset contribution level
no data on persistence beyond the study window
relevance_reason: RCT showing that a nudge in a consumer financial setting improves average outcomes while harming a specific vulnerable subgroup, directly informing the distributional-risk question the brief raises about defaulting everyone in.
